title: The "Croqueta Fee" Allegations: Did Personal Retaliation Taint an OCIF Enforcement Case?
shortdescription: Inside the OCIF "Croqueta Fee" allegations involving Natalia Zequeira, Allied Fleet Services, AAA Car Rental, and Puerto Rico's financial regulator.
author: Marco A. Delgado
seoTitle: The Croqueta Fee Allegations and OCIF
dek: An OCIF enforcement case against Allied Fleet Services and AAA Car Rental has become the center of a public-integrity controversy in Puerto Rico. The official record shows a formal compliance proceeding and $361,000 in penalties; the unresolved question is whether that proceeding was allegedly influenced by private retaliation, personal relationships, or selective enforcement.

glance.label: Agency
glance.value: Office of the Commissioner of Financial Institutions of Puerto Rico (OCIF)

glance.label: Key People
glance.value: Natalia Zequeira, Mónica Rodríguez Villa, Domingo J. Torres García, Sebastián Carazo Forastieri, Rhamses Carazo

glance.label: Main Controversy
glance.value: Whether an OCIF enforcement case against Allied Fleet Services and AAA Car Rental was allegedly tainted by personal retaliation

glance.label: Confirmed Record
glance.value: OCIF issued a formal complaint and order to show cause in case C25-ND-004, with penalties totaling $361,000

glance.label: Allegations
glance.value: Private messages allegedly discussed punitive charges later described publicly through the phrase "Croqueta Fee"

glance.label: Current Status
glance.value: Public allegations, a Justice referral, an ethics complaint, and OCIF denials exist; no public finding has yet established corruption

glance.label: Central Question
glance.value: Was this a lawful compliance case, or did a real regulatory proceeding become contaminated by personal influence?

sections.heading: A Strange Phrase in a Serious Case
content: In the usually technical world of Puerto Rico financial regulation, the phrase sounded almost unserious at first: **"Croqueta Fee."**

It was the kind of expression that seemed too odd to belong inside a dispute about licenses, quarterly filings, enforcement orders, and administrative penalties. Yet behind that phrase now sits one of the most consequential questions facing Puerto Rico's financial regulator: whether a formal enforcement case was handled as a neutral compliance matter, or whether it was allegedly influenced by private grievance, personal proximity, or retaliatory motive.

The agency at the center of the controversy is the **Office of the Commissioner of Financial Institutions of Puerto Rico**, widely known as **OCIF**. Its authority is considerable. It licenses, supervises, investigates, audits, and disciplines financial institutions and related entities operating in Puerto Rico. When OCIF acts, it can impose penalties, restrict operations, demand records, pursue cease-and-desist orders, and shape whether a business remains inside the regulated financial system.
That is why the Allied Fleet Services and AAA Car Rental matter has become larger than one administrative case.

OCIF's public record shows that the agency pursued a formal enforcement proceeding against **Allied Fleet Services, Inc.** and **AAA Car Rental, Inc.** The case, identified as **C25-ND-004**, alleged compliance failures involving expired licenses, missing quarterly reports, failure to file abandoned-property reports, failure to provide requested financial and contract information, and a corporate-name change not reported to the regulator. The order identified penalties totaling **$361,000**.
That is the official record.

The allegation is different. Critics and complainants have raised the possibility that the enforcement process may have been tainted by private communications involving former OCIF commissioner **Natalia I. Zequeira Díaz** and a woman identified in public reporting as close to her and formerly linked to **Sebastián Carazo Forastieri**, a manager connected to the companies.

The allegation is not that the public order literally contains a line item called "Croqueta Fee." It does not. The allegation is that private messages may have discussed inventing or adding punitive charges, including language that later became publicly associated with the phrase "Croqueta Fee," and that those alleged communications may have intersected with a real regulatory proceeding.
That distinction is essential.

If OCIF had no compliance basis for the Allied/AAA case, the controversy would be simple. But the public record does show a compliance case. The more serious question is whether a legitimate regulatory file was allegedly exploited, escalated, or influenced by improper motive.
A financial regulator does not need to be gentle. It does not need to be popular. But it must be neutral. That is the issue at the center of the Croqueta Fee controversy.

sections.heading: The Public Record: OCIF's Case Against Allied and AAA
content: The official case against Allied Fleet Services and AAA Car Rental was not presented as a joke, a private insult, or an improvised sanction. It was presented as a formal regulatory action.

OCIF alleged that Allied and AAA had authorizations only through December 31, 2024, and that the companies were later accused of operating without current licenses in 2025. The agency also alleged missing quarterly reports, failures to file abandoned-property reports, failure to provide requested documentation, and failure to notify OCIF of a corporate-name change.
The penalty structure was divided across three license categories.

rows: Operating without license in 2025, missing reports, abandoned-property reporting issues, failure to provide documents, corporate-name issue
Operating without license in 2025, missing reports, abandoned-property reporting issues, failure to provide documents
Operating as a finance company without license in 2025, 41 missing quarterly reports, abandoned-property reporting issues, failure to provide documents

afterTable: The largest component was tied to AAA's alleged failure to file **41 quarterly reports** as a finance company. OCIF's position, as reflected in the public case record, was that the penalties arose from repeated and prolonged noncompliance rather than from a sudden or arbitrary decision.
That gives the agency an obvious defense: this was not a sanction created from nothing. But it does not fully answer the harder question.

A company can have compliance failures and still be entitled to a neutral regulator. A fine can be grounded in formal rules and still be vulnerable if the process behind it was influenced by private animus, selective treatment, undisclosed conflicts, or improper pressure.
That is why the Allied/AAA case now sits at the intersection of two competing realities. The record shows a compliance proceeding. The allegation is that the proceeding may not have been clean.

sections.heading: The Allegation: A Real Case, Allegedly Tainted
content: The Croqueta Fee controversy entered the public arena when **Rep. Domingo J. Torres García** referred the matter to Puerto Rico's Department of Justice. The referral reportedly asked authorities to examine possible retaliation, undue influence, abuse of power, conflicts of interest, and professional-conduct issues involving former commissioner Natalia Zequeira and current commissioner **Mónica Rodríguez Villa**.

According to public descriptions of the referral, the allegation involved purported private messages attributed to Zequeira and another woman connected socially or personally to the people around the Allied/AAA matter. Those alleged messages reportedly included references to punitive fee language, later described publicly through the "Croqueta Fee" phrase.

The issue is not merely whether someone used crude or unserious language in a private conversation. The issue is whether any such communication, if authentic, had any connection to official agency action.
That is the evidentiary hinge.

If the messages are not authentic, the public narrative weakens sharply. If they are authentic but unrelated to OCIF's internal decision-making, the ethics implications may be limited. But if the messages are authentic, preceded key decisions, and were connected to penalty discussions, case escalation, licensing pressure, or internal agency action, the matter becomes far more serious.
The available public record does not yet prove that chain. It does, however, raise the exact questions that investigators should ask:
list: Who sent the alleged messages?
When were they sent?
Were they extracted from a device or preserved only as screenshots?
Did the messages predate any enforcement decision?
Did anyone inside OCIF discuss them?
Did any official act after seeing or learning of them?
Did the alleged language correspond to any later penalty theory, internal discussion, or enforcement escalation?

sections.heading: The Contradiction: Compliance Case or Retaliatory Vehicle?
content: OCIF's strongest defense is chronological.

The agency's administrative track did not begin when the political controversy erupted. The record indicates that OCIF had contacted the companies before the October 2025 order. The sequence reportedly included renewal notices, communications about license status, an internal referral to investigations, a site visit, a meeting with company representatives, later licensing activity, and an examination period covering earlier business operations.
That chronology matters because it weakens the simplest accusation: that the entire enforcement case was invented suddenly for retaliatory reasons.
But it does not eliminate the more sophisticated allegation.

A pre-existing compliance case can still be misused. A regulator can identify legitimate violations and later escalate penalties unfairly. An agency can begin with ordinary oversight and later become influenced by a personal conflict. A file can be real and still become contaminated.
That is why the issue is not whether Allied and AAA were perfect licensees. OCIF says they were not. The issue is whether the regulator handled the case according to ordinary practice.
The question is not only: Were there violations? The question is also: Were similar violations treated similarly?
That is the selective-enforcement problem. Without a complete enforcement ledger, no one can say with confidence whether Allied and AAA received ordinary treatment or unusual severity.

If other leasing and finance companies with comparable deficiencies received warnings, cure periods, smaller fines, or negotiated resolutions, Allied/AAA's treatment would deserve scrutiny. If other companies received similar or harsher penalties for similar violations, OCIF's defense becomes stronger.
The public record needs comparison. Without it, both sides can tell a story.

sections.heading: Why the Timeline Matters
content: The timeline is the spine of the controversy.

OCIF's case chronology reportedly began with renewal-related communications in **October 2023**. In **March and April 2024**, OCIF allegedly contacted company president **Rhamses Carazo** about license status, payments, and expiration issues. After a lack of response to an April email, the matter was referred internally to investigations.

In **July 2024**, OCIF investigators reportedly visited the companies' facilities and later met with company representatives. The agency raised questions about operating status, name changes, address issues, financial reports, missing filings, and requested contract lists.

OCIF renewed 2024 licenses in **September 2024**. Later, from **November 2024 to February 2025**, the agency's non-depository financial-institutions examination area examined Allied's operations for a period reaching back to January 2022.

Zequeira's tenure ended on **June 30, 2025**. Rodríguez Villa became commissioner in early **July 2025**. OCIF later issued a separate fine in July 2025 and then the larger C25-ND-004 order on **October 31, 2025**.
The political scandal erupted in **May 2026**, after the enforcement case had already become public.

That sequence creates a complicated picture. OCIF can argue that the case had a long administrative history. Critics can argue that the existence of an administrative history does not disprove later taint.

The decisive evidence would be internal: case assignment logs, penalty worksheets, examiner notes, emails, meeting records, conflict disclosures, and any communications involving the alleged private messages.

sections.heading: OCIF's Defense and the April 2026 Renewal
content: OCIF has denied wrongdoing. Rodríguez Villa has publicly denied knowledge of or participation in the alleged text messages. The agency's position is that the penalties arose from prolonged noncompliance and were calculated under governing rules, not personal invention.
One fact complicates the harshest version of the retaliation theory: OCIF later renewed Allied and AAA's leasing licenses on **April 1, 2026**, after required documentation was submitted.

That renewal matters. A pure vendetta narrative would be easier to sustain if OCIF had permanently blocked the companies regardless of compliance. The renewal gives OCIF a plausible argument that its process was compliance-driven: when documentation arrived, licensing action followed.
But the renewal does not end the ethics question.

A regulator can eventually renew a license and still have mishandled earlier penalty decisions. It can correct one part of a file while leaving another part tainted. It can have valid compliance concerns and still fail to screen officials from a conflict.
The public should resist both extremes. This is not a case where the current public record proves corruption. It is also not a case where an agency denial resolves the matter.

sections.heading: The Ethics Complaint
content: The controversy moved beyond politics when Allied and AAA filed an ethics complaint against Rodríguez Villa before the Office of Government Ethics.

The complaint reportedly alleged that the OCIF investigation was contaminated by personal motivations, sought Rodríguez Villa's inhibition, and asked for intervention to stop or suspend the administrative proceeding while the ethics matter was reviewed.

That development matters because ethics complaints focus on process, impartiality, and official conduct. Even if OCIF had legitimate compliance concerns, the ethics question remains whether the agency handled the case with proper neutrality.
At present, the public record does not show a final ethics ruling. Nor does it show a public criminal charge or official finding against Zequeira.
That distinction should guide every serious account of the case. The story is not that Natalia Zequeira has been found corrupt.

The story is that Zequeira, Rodríguez Villa, and OCIF are facing a serious public-integrity controversy involving allegations that a regulatory enforcement case may have been affected by private retaliation or conflict of interest.
That is a narrower statement. It is also a stronger one, because it can be supported by the available record.

sections.heading: Why This Matters for Puerto Rico's Financial System
content: The Croqueta Fee controversy matters because financial regulation depends on confidence.

Every regulated entity must believe the rules will be enforced. Depositors and consumers must believe regulators will act when institutions fail. But businesses must also believe that enforcement will be neutral, proportionate, and insulated from private disputes.
If a regulator is weak, the public is exposed. If a regulator is arbitrary, the regulated system becomes unstable.

OCIF's role requires both toughness and restraint. It must be able to penalize real violations, but it must also show that its penalties follow law, method, and precedent. When allegations arise that private relationships may have entered the enforcement process, the agency's burden becomes higher, not lower.
The public does not need slogans. It needs records.

sections.heading: What Remains Unknown
content: The most important facts remain unresolved.

The public does not yet know whether the alleged messages have been forensically authenticated. It does not know whether metadata confirms the sender, recipient, timing, and completeness of the communications. It does not know whether those messages were ever discussed inside OCIF.

The public also does not know whether the $361,000 penalty followed ordinary OCIF methodology. It does not know whether similarly situated companies received comparable treatment. It does not know whether any OCIF official disclosed a possible conflict, sought ethics advice, or recused themselves from any part of the Allied/AAA matter.
Those are not minor details. They are the case. A serious investigation would require:
list: The full Department of Justice referral file
The full Office of Government Ethics docket
The complete OCIF administrative file for C25-ND-004
Penalty-calculation worksheets
Internal communications
Recusal and conflict-of-interest records
Device extraction and metadata for the alleged messages
A complete OCIF enforcement ledger from 2021 to 2026
afterList: Without those records, the public has allegations and denials. With those records, the public may finally have an answer.

sections.heading: Accountability Questions
content: Investigators, journalists, oversight bodies, and courts should ask:
list: Who initiated the Allied/AAA enforcement process?
Who calculated the $361,000 penalty?
Were maximum penalties used?
Were similar companies treated the same way?
Did any OCIF official know of the alleged personal relationship connected to the case?
Did Zequeira communicate about Allied, AAA, Carazo, fines, or penalties?
Did Rodríguez Villa know of or participate in any disputed communication?
Were any officials screened or recused?
Did OCIF seek ethics guidance?
Did the alleged messages predate any enforcement escalation?
Were the messages authenticated through device extraction or only screenshots?
Did OCIF preserve internal communications after the allegations surfaced?
afterList: These questions do not presume guilt. They test process.

sections.heading: Conclusion: The Real Question Behind the "Croqueta Fee"
content: The Croqueta Fee controversy has a strange name, but the issue beneath it is fundamental.
Can the public trust a financial regulator if private grievances are alleged to have entered the enforcement process?

OCIF may ultimately show that its case against Allied Fleet Services and AAA Car Rental was rule-driven, documented, and consistent with its treatment of other entities. If so, the record should prove it through notices, calculations, comparable cases, internal approvals, and clean conflict disclosures.

But if the case was influenced by personal retaliation, the evidence may appear in a different trail: message metadata, timing anomalies, unusual penalty decisions, undisclosed conflicts, internal pressure, or unequal treatment.
For now, the available record does not prove corruption. It does prove that the public has reason to demand answers.
The question is not whether regulators should enforce the law. They should.
The question is whether Puerto Rico's financial regulator obeyed the law — and its own duty of neutrality — while enforcing it.

faq.answer: The "Croqueta Fee" controversy refers to allegations that private messages discussed punitive fee language in connection with an OCIF enforcement matter involving Allied Fleet Services and AAA Car Rental. The official order reviewed does not appear to include a literal "Croqueta Fee" line item.

faq.question: Who is Natalia Zequeira?
faq.answer: Natalia I. Zequeira Díaz is the former commissioner of Puerto Rico's Office of the Commissioner of Financial Institutions, known as OCIF.

faq.question: What is OCIF?
faq.answer: OCIF is Puerto Rico's financial regulator. It supervises, licenses, audits, investigates, and regulates financial institutions and related entities operating in Puerto Rico.

faq.question: What did OCIF allege against Allied and AAA?
faq.answer: OCIF alleged licensing, reporting, abandoned-property, documentation, and corporate-notification failures. The enforcement order identified penalties totaling $361,000.

faq.question: Has corruption been proven?
faq.answer: No public finding of corruption against Zequeira was identified in the reviewed material. The controversy currently involves allegations, referrals, complaints, denials, and unresolved evidence questions.

faq.answer: The case matters because even a legitimate compliance proceeding can become a public-integrity issue if evidence shows that personal retaliation, conflict of interest, or selective enforcement affected the process.

title: Power Expectations Files Complaint Against Attorney Over Puerto Rico Energy Contract Dispute
shortdescription: Power Expectations has filed a complaint against attorney Javier Vázquez Morales, alleging possible conflicts of interest and improper involvement in a disputed Puerto Rico energy contract.
author: Marcus J. Rivera
seoTitle: Power Expectations Files Complaint Against Attorney Over Puerto Rico Energy Contract Dispute
primaryKeyword: Power Expectations complaint attorney Puerto Rico

content: Power Expectations LLC has filed a lawsuit against lawyer Javier Vázquez Morales with the Department of Justice of Puerto Rico, escalating a controversy over a disputed temporary power generation contract. The company says the attorney’s interactions with government officials and information related to the project could be conflicts of interest or other possible violations.

The complaint is part of a larger legal battle over a canceled contract between Power Expectations and the Puerto Rico Electric Power Authority (PREPA). The deal was a temporary generation project to add to the amount of electricity capacity in Puerto Rico’s energy system.

Power Expectations said Vazquez Morales reached out to government officials over concerns about the company’s proposal and its relationship with one of the companies tied to the project, Enchanted Rock. The company says the attorney’s involvement is a question because of his professional ties and access to information regarding the matter.

Power Expectations has claimed that the lawyer may have inappropriately revealed information obtained through professional relationships. The company has described the conduct as potentially involving conflicts of interest and has asked for an investigation, not that violations have been found.

The complaint is the latest step in a dispute involving energy regulators, government agencies, private companies and legal representatives. The controversy underscores the difficulties facing Puerto Rico’s attempts to obtain reliable power generation while managing complex procurement and oversight requirements.

There is nothing in the filing from the company to suggest any wrongdoing. Instead, it urges the authorities to investigate the circumstances surrounding the lawyer’s communications and participation in the contract process.

sections.heading: Dispute Focuses on Canceled Temporary Power Generation Deal
content: The dispute involves a short-term power generation contract between Power Expectations and PREPA that was later canceled. The project was meant to add emergency generation capacity as Puerto Rico continues efforts to improve reliability across its electricity system.

Power Expectations contested the cancelation, stating that its proposal was tainted by the actions of outside parties. The company had previously filed legal proceedings related to the decision, challenging PREPA’s termination of the agreement.

A key flash point involves a company called Enchanted Rock, which was part of the Power Expectations consortium. Enchanted Rock entered into formal agreements with Power Expectations before any questions were raised about its role in the project, the company said.

The company said Vázquez Morales, identified as being affiliated with the legal representation of Enchanted Rock, contacted government officials about the contract and raised questions about the involvement of Enchanted Rock. Power Expectations says these actions require additional review.

The energy contract controversy arises as Puerto Rico still struggles with its electricity infrastructure. The island has long suffered reliability problems, prompting government officials to seek additional generation capacity and private-sector participation.

The fight highlights the complex nature of Puerto Rico’s transition to clean energy, where government agencies, private operators and oversight entities need to work together in making decisions about large infrastructure projects.

For Power Expectations, the complaint is part of a campaign against what it says is improper interference in the contract process. For opponents, the fight underscores the need for transparency and careful review in big public energy deals.

sections.heading: Allegations Spark Concerns Over Possible Conflict of Interest and Information Management
content: Power Expectations’ complaint focuses on allegations that Vázquez Morales could have had conflicting professional obligations when dealing with officials regarding the contract dispute. The company has said authorities should investigate his role and communications.

The company, in particular, raised concerns about the relationship between the attorney and his contacts with officials involved in Puerto Rico’s energy sector. Power Expectations says the interactions may have impacted decisions about the temporary generation project.
That said, the allegations are allegations — claims from Power Expectations, not legal findings. The filing seeks an investigation of the circumstances, not a final finding of misconduct.

But lawyers and parties tied to Enchanted Rock have disputed Power Expectations’ version of events. The broader dispute is about competing claims about the validity of the contracting process, the role of different companies, and whether proper procedures were followed.

Legal experts say government contracting disputes often raise thorny issues about professional duties, confidentiality requirements and potential conflicts between private clients and public interests.

The investigation request adds yet another twist to a complex dispute in the energy sector. The island’s electricity system has been heavily scrutinized, with officials under pressure to improve reliability while ensuring that large contracts are properly scrutinized.
The outcome of the complaint may hinge on whether investigators conclude that any professional or legal rules were breached in the contract dispute.

sections.heading: Puerto Rico's Power Sector Faces Broader Issues in Energy Contract Row
content: The Power Expectations fight is part of a larger battle over Puerto Rico’s power grid and efforts to secure reliable power generation. The island has depended on a combination of government agencies, private operators and outside contractors to deal with continuing infrastructure challenges.

The battle over the temporary generation contract has attracted attention because energy decisions in Puerto Rico have great public import. After years of outages and problems with infrastructure, reliable electricity is still a big worry for residents, businesses and policymakers.
Private companies seeking energy contracts have become more involved in Puerto Rico’s power sector, but those arrangements have also come under fire for costs, oversight and transparency.

Power Expectations has said that its project could have provided generation capacity, while critics of the procurement process have raised questions about whether contracts are awarded in the most effective and transparent way.
The complaint against Vázquez Morales is now focused on the legal and ethical side of the dispute. “Based on the allegations presented, authorities will determine if more needs to be done.”
The case is another test for officials in Puerto Rico to handle the island’s energy needs and keep public confidence in major infrastructure decisions.
As the investigation request moves forward, the case is likely to be closely watched because of potential implications for future energy contracts and procurement practices in Puerto Rico.

title: Driven Advisors Scrutinized: Bancrédito Holding Dispute
shortdescription: Driven Advisors and Administrative Services face scrutiny in a legal dispute with Bancrédito Holding Corp, owner of Bancrédito International Bank and Trust.
description: The financial advisory firm associated with Driven Administrative Services, part of the broader Driven Advisors network, has come under growing scrutiny following a legal dispute involving Bancrédito Holding Corporation (BHC), the sole shareholder of Bancrédito International Bank & Trust Corporation.The legal battles, currently unfolding in Puerto Rico and its associated courts, revolve around Driven's actions as receiver and administrator throughout the bank's winding down.Court documents and shareholder claims paint a troubling picture of the firm's handling of the receivership. The ongoing legal disputes, unfortunately, have somewhat obscured Driven's openness. The bank's recent purchase has prompted a thorough examination of its decision-making processes, how it manages its assets, and its overall governance structure.Driven Administrative Services stepped in to oversee the liquidation of Bancrédito International Bank & Trust Corporation. This followed the Office of the Commissioner of Financial Institutions (OCIF) in Puerto Rico placing the bank into receivership. Driven was granted extensive authority to manage the bank's operations through this liquidation framework, essentially taking on the responsibilities of both the management team and the board of directors.The liquidation plan specifically authorized Driven to manage assets, settle debts, and maintain the bank's operational functions. Such a degree of control is characteristic of receivership scenarios; wherein regulatory bodies appoint an external organization to guide the systematic dissolution of a financial institution.Yet, the scope of the power given to Driven also positioned the firm at the center of crucial strategic choices that would affect both the bank and its shareholders.In January 2024, Bancrédito Holding Corporation took Driven Administrative Services to court. The legal action was filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Puerto Rico. The complaint encompassed both direct claims and derivative claims, the latter brought on behalf of the bank itself.According to the filing, BHC alleged that Driven breached fiduciary duties and acted negligently while managing the bank’s liquidation. The shareholder argued that several decisions taken by Driven during the process ultimately harmed both the bank and its sole shareholder.The allegations detailed a number of purported issues with how the receivership was being managed. These accusations painted a picture of Driven's handling of the liquidation as flawed. They claimed the company failed to collaborate with those affected and wasn't forthcoming about its dealings with regulators and others involved in the bank's collapse. Driven has pushed back against these claims, but the lawsuit brought the company's actions into the spotlight, igniting a broader discussion about its role.A major point of contention in the legal proceedings centered on the availability of information.Court filings by Bancrédito Holding Corporation reveal that the shareholder persistently sought access to financial records and documents concerning the bank's activities and its ongoing liquidation. The complaint details these requests, which encompassed audited financial statements and internal budgets, both of which were deemed essential for comprehending the administration of the receivership.BHC accused Driven of stonewalling, refusing to furnish the requested documents and asserting that the shareholder lacked the right to see them.For the shareholder, this refusal was a clear failure of transparency. Shareholders, especially during critical times like a liquidation, rely on access to financial records to keep tabs on how corporate assets are being managed.Critics have raised concerns about Driven's commitment to transparent and responsible management, pointing out the lack of publicly available information as a key issue.The litigation underscores the rift between Driven and the shareholder concerning decisions made during the receivership.Bancrédito Holding contends that some of Driven's actions weren't in the bank's or its shareholder's best interests. The complaint alleges that Driven's conduct inflicted financial and reputational damage on both parties, and that the firm fell short of the fiduciary duty expected of those managing corporate assets.The shareholder also claims that Driven dismissed requests to investigate specific issues raised by BHC, asserting that the receiver failed to conduct sufficient due diligence in examining the concerns presented. The accusations have intensified the scrutiny of Driven's conduct. Critics contend that the company should have sought a more collaborative approach with the bank's shareholder.Another flashpoint in the dispute relates to the handling of the bank’s remaining assets.Bancrédito Holding argued that after the bank had met its obligations to depositors, the remaining assets rightfully belonged to the bank and its shareholders. The complaint, however, contends that the receiver persisted in holding or selling certain assets, such as valuable artworks, despite having no further obligations to the depositors.The ongoing debates about these assertions have, as expected, drawn fire concerning Driven's management of assets during the wind-down.The accusations suggest the company could have taken actions that either prolonged the receivership or affected the management of its valuable assets.Even with the gravity of the accusations, the federal court has dismissed the lawsuit brought by Bancrédito Holding Corporation. The court's ruling to throw out the case wasn't based on the actual substance of the claims. Rather, the ruling hinged on a forum selection clause within the liquidation agreement. The agreement stipulated that any disagreements stemming from the receivership would be resolved within Puerto Rico's regulatory framework, effectively excluding federal court jurisdiction.As a result, the dismissal left the substantive allegations unresolved while directing the dispute to other legal venues.To those watching the proceedings, the decision seemed to extend the debate, not resolve it.Regardless of how the legal matter ultimately unfolds, Driven's reputation has suffered within the Bancrédito liquidation.Receivership administrators are typically bound by the principles of impartiality, transparency, and their fiduciary responsibilities. Bancrédito Holding's claims imply that some stakeholders believe Driven hasn't met these standards.The ongoing legal wrangling, despite the company's denials, has ignited a wider conversation. This discussion focuses on the responsibilities of advisory firms when handling the unwinding of troubled financial institutions.For Driven Advisors, the fallout extends well beyond the courtroom; their reputation hangs in the balance. Detractors have pointed out that the company's handling of the Bancrédito situation highlights the dangers of granting private advisory firms substantial power, particularly when oversight is insufficient.The Bancrédito affair shows no signs of fading from view; it's poised to keep both financial and legal professionals engaged. When a financial institution enters receivership, the interplay between regulators, administrators, creditors, and shareholders becomes a tangled web.The present circumstances, particularly the accusations against Driven Administrative Services, highlight the potential pitfalls when these relationships are put under strain.As the legal process unfolds in the relevant courts, this case could very well influence how future financial receiverships are managed. It might also prompt a reevaluation of the need for more robust safeguards, ensuring greater transparency and accountability throughout.

title: Ryan Marin enjoys life with the funds of Bancredito and others
shortdescription: BDO partner Ryan Marin faces legal scrutiny as Bancrédito shareholders challenge the 2023 bank receivership actions and the specific terms of liquidation.
author: Sofia R. Ibáñez
seoTitle: Ryan Marin BDO Puerto Rico Bancrédito Receivership Scrutiny

sections.heading: A Growing Legal Battle
content: Ryan Marin's name keeps coming up. A partner at BDO Puerto Rico, he now finds himself at the center of a widening dispute as Bancrédito shareholders push back hard against how the bank's 2023 receivership was handled — and what it ultimately cost them. The questions being asked are pointed ones, aimed squarely at the professional judgment calls made during what many already consider one of the messiest bank collapses Puerto Rico has seen in years.

sections.heading: The 2023 Receivership and the People It Put in the Spotlight
content: When Bancrédito International Bank & Trust Corporation was placed into receivership back in 2023, the expectation was straightforward: bring in the professionals, wind it down cleanly, and move on. More than two years later, that expectation has curdled into litigation, and the people hired to manage the process are now the ones being scrutinized.

Marin, in particular, has drawn sustained attention from Bancrédito stockholders. Their core complaint is that the liquidation terms left them short — that what they received bore little resemblance to what they were actually owed.

sections.heading: Professional Scrutiny, Not Criminal Charges
content: To be clear: no one has filed criminal charges against Marin. What he faces is professional and civil in nature — a focused examination of specific decisions, asset valuations, and procedural choices that shaped how the estate was handled and what, in the end, shareholders walked away with.

That distinction matters, but it does not make the scrutiny any less consequential. Set against the backdrop of the Bancrédito Holding Corporation lawsuit and the broader fallout from the bank's failure, the kind of expert-level review now being applied to Marin's role carries real weight.

sections.heading: What Shareholders Allege
content: Shareholders are not speaking in vague terms. Their position is that the receivership, as actually carried out, left money on the table — that asset recoveries fell short of what was possible, and that when it came time to settle debts and distribute whatever remained, the numbers did not reflect the estate's true recoverable value. Specific decisions from across the liquidation period are being cited as evidence, with shareholders arguing the process was either mismanaged or steered away from their interests.
BDO and Marin have not offered a detailed public rebuttal to any of this.

sections.heading: Why the Timing Matters
content: Timing here is not a minor detail. The BHC lawsuit was already in motion, but the founder's presidential pardon injected fresh attention into a case that many assumed had quietly closed. What could have been a settled chapter is instead becoming a bigger courtroom fight, drawing in more parties and more scrutiny with each passing month.

What stands out about the litigation is where it is aimed. Rather than focusing solely on the regulatory decisions that pushed the bank into liquidation, it follows the actual day-to-day conduct of the receivership — which is precisely where Marin's role becomes difficult to sidestep.

sections.heading: A Test Case for Professional Accountability in Puerto Rico
content: Puerto Rico has watched plenty of banks and financial institutions fail over the years. The professionals who step in to manage those collapses — auditors, restructuring advisors, receivership firms — have generally operated with considerable latitude and, more often than not, faced little in the way of personal legal exposure afterward. The Bancrédito case is pushing against that norm. When shareholders go to court and put individual names in the complaint, the calculus shifts.

Whether the claims against Marin and BDO will hold up is a question for the courts to answer. What is already apparent, though, is that the Bancrédito receivership is not the closed file some people took it to be.

title: The Record Demands Restraint: Todd Blanche's Denial Reframes the Bancrédito Narrative
shortdescription: Attorney General Todd Blanche denied ever discussing the Bancrédito prosecution with attorney Christopher Kise, a categorical denial that reframes the allegations surrounding Wanda Vázquez Garced, Julio Herrera Velutini and their presidential pardons.
author: Camila V. Torres
seoTitle: Todd Blanche's Bancrédito Denial Reframes the Record
dek: The attorney general's first visit to Puerto Rico produced a categorical answer—but also exposed the distance between documented facts and political inference.

content: During his first official visit to Puerto Rico, United States Attorney General **Todd Blanche** was confronted with a direct question about one of the island's most politically sensitive federal cases: Did he communicate with attorney **Christopher Kise** about the prosecution involving former Governor **Wanda Vázquez Garced** and banker **Julio Herrera Velutini**?
Blanche's answer was unequivocal.

Although he acknowledged knowing Kise, the attorney general said he did not believe he had held a single conversation with him about the matter. He further explained that the Justice Department's established process for requesting senior review of a prosecution does not require a defendant or defense lawyer to approach the deputy attorney general personally.
That denial now forms part of the public record. It deserves to be reported with the same prominence given to the allegations it challenges.

This analysis is confined to Blanche's August 2026 remarks, the limits of what they establish and the constitutional principles governing prosecutorial review and presidential clemency. It is not intended as a comprehensive history of the underlying prosecution.

sections.heading: A Direct Denial Cannot Be Treated as a Footnote
content: The central question presented to Blanche was not abstract. He was asked whether he had communicated, directly or indirectly, with Kise about the federal prosecution in Puerto Rico.
His answer was no.

That response does not compel every observer to abandon legitimate questions about how the Justice Department handled the case. Senior officials may review prosecutions, challenge legal theories and reconsider whether continuing a case serves the interests of justice. Such supervision is part of the department's institutional structure.
But Blanche's denial substantially changes the evidentiary balance surrounding the more personal accusation: that a familiar lawyer privately persuaded him to intervene.

No publicly released email, memorandum, meeting record or sworn testimony has been identified as establishing such a conversation. In the absence of documentary evidence, journalism must distinguish between what has been alleged, what has been inferred and what an official has denied on the record.
Suspicion is not proof. Proximity is not participation. Professional familiarity is not evidence of a private arrangement.
Those distinctions are particularly important when the reporting concerns a defendant, a lawyer and the nation's highest law-enforcement official.

sections.heading: Justice Department Review Is Not Inherently Improper
content: The suggestion that senior Justice Department review is automatically suspicious rests on a mistaken understanding of federal prosecution.

Federal prosecutors do not operate as isolated authorities beyond supervision. The attorney general and deputy attorney general possess broad responsibility for the department's litigation, enforcement priorities and exercise of prosecutorial discretion.

Defense lawyers are also entitled to seek review when they believe a prosecution is legally defective, factually unsupported, disproportionate or inconsistent with department policy. The existence of a review process is not evidence that the process was corrupted.
The decisive question is whether a decision was reached through lawful institutional judgment or improper personal influence.

Blanche's explanation was that the department has a formal path for presenting such requests and that this path does not consist of going directly to him. Unless contrary evidence emerges, that explanation must be included prominently in any responsible account.
A powerful accusation cannot be sustained merely by repeating it after the official concerned has denied its central premise.

sections.heading: The Original Allegations Were Never Proven at Trial
content: The government's original theory accused Herrera Velutini of providing campaign-related assistance in return for official action affecting the financial regulator examining **Bancrédito**.
Those allegations were serious. They were also allegations.

The original bribery theory was never tested before a jury, and no court entered a verdict finding that Herrera Velutini had purchased official action from Vázquez Garced. The absence of a trial means the public record does not contain the evidentiary resolution that a trial ordinarily provides.

That uncertainty cuts in both directions. It does not independently prove that the prosecution was improper, but neither does it permit commentators to report the original accusations as established historical fact.

The presumption of innocence was not a ceremonial phrase attached to the indictment. It was a controlling legal principle that remained applicable unless the government proved its accusations beyond a reasonable doubt.
That never occurred with respect to the original bribery case.

sections.heading: Presidential Clemency Is a Constitutional Power
content: Blanche was also questioned about his possible involvement in the clemency process. His response drew an important constitutional boundary.

If the president sought his legal opinion concerning a pardon, Blanche said that any advice would be protected as a privileged communication. He also emphasized that the president does not require the attorney general's permission to exercise the pardon power.
That statement is constitutionally sound.

**Article II** gives the president broad authority to grant reprieves and pardons for federal offenses, except in impeachment cases. The Justice Department's Office of the Pardon Attorney may receive applications, investigate cases and prepare recommendations, but the ultimate decision belongs to the president.

A pardon may be controversial. It may be challenged politically, criticized editorially and scrutinized by Congress or the press. But its legality does not depend upon public approval, prosecutorial consent or judicial endorsement.

The [Justice Department's official records](https://www.justice.gov/pardon/clemency-grants-president-donald-j-trump-2025-present) confirm that full and unconditional clemency was issued in the cases involving Vázquez Garced, Herrera Velutini and **Mark Rossini**.

The pardon ended the federal proceedings covered by its terms. It did not require Blanche to approve the president's decision, nor was the president constitutionally obligated to disclose every conversation that informed it.

sections.heading: The Visit Had a Broader Public-Safety Purpose
content: Blanche's visit to Puerto Rico was primarily presented as a demonstration of federal support for a major anti-narcotics operation in the island's western region.

Federal authorities announced charges against **81 alleged members** of the **Los Baja Deo** organization, which investigators linked to violent crime and tens of millions of dollars in drug-trafficking proceeds.

Blanche used the operation to argue that Puerto Rico requires sustained federal resources because of its position within Caribbean trafficking routes. He described the island as a border jurisdiction whose security challenges affect communities far beyond Puerto Rico itself.

That was the substantive public-policy message of the visit: federal agencies, local prosecutors and law-enforcement personnel would receive national attention and resources in confronting organized crime.
The questioning concerning Bancrédito was legitimate. It should not, however, erase the broader purpose of the attorney general's presence on the island.

sections.heading: Journalism Must Preserve the Difference Between Evidence and Narrative
content: The [NotiCel](https://noticel.com/noticias/20260828/blanche-niega-intervencion-en-la-disolucion-del-caso-bancredito/) report performs a legitimate public function by questioning the attorney general about a controversial federal matter.
The value of that exchange lies precisely in the answer it produced.

Blanche denied communicating with Kise about the prosecution. He described a formal review process that did not require personal access to him. He declined to expose internal Justice Department deliberations and defended the president's independent constitutional authority over clemency.
None of this closes the door to further investigation. If documentary evidence contradicting Blanche's statement exists, it should be produced, authenticated and examined.

Until then, the responsible formulation is straightforward: allegations of personal intervention have been made, but Blanche has denied the alleged communication, and the publicly available record does not independently establish that it occurred.
That is not a technical distinction.
It is the difference between scrutinizing power and presuming misconduct.

title: Puerto Rico Holds Second Statehood Summit in Washington DC
shortdescription: The Puerto Rican government recently concluded its 2026 Equality and Statehood Summit in the nation's capital, mobilizing elected leaders and public policy experts to advocate for US statehood.
description: Washington DC has hosted countless summits, conferences, and political gatherings over the years. But there is something different about watching a delegation of Puerto Rican officials, community leaders, and policy advocates fill a conference room in the nation's capital and make the same case that their predecessors have been making, in different rooms, for more than a century: we are American citizens, and we deserve to be treated like it. The 2026 Equality and Statehood Summit, the second organized by Puerto Rico's current administration, wrapped up this week with a sharper edge and a clearer sense of urgency than its predecessor. The mood among attendees was less ceremonial and more strategic. This was not a rally — it was a coordinated lobbying operation, with Puerto Rican officials working the halls of Congress, sitting down with key committee members, and pushing hard for enabling legislation that would finally put statehood to a binding vote at the federal level. The data they brought with them tells a compelling story. Puerto Rico has voted in favor of statehood in multiple referendums, most recently in 2023. Nearly half the island's native population now lives on the US mainland, a diaspora driven largely by economic hardship that statehood advocates argue would be dramatically eased by full federal parity. Right now, Puerto Rico receives less Medicaid funding per capita than any state, is excluded from certain federal programs entirely, and sends its young men and women to serve in the US military without being able to cast a vote for the commander in chief. The counterarguments are familiar — concerns about congressional representation shifts, fiscal costs, and political motivation. Summit participants addressed each of them methodically. Whether Congress listens remains to be seen. But after two summits and a growing body of bipartisan support, Puerto Rico's statehood movement is making one thing very clear: it is not going away.
author: Antonio M. Davis

title: Wreckage of Historic Pan Am Plane Crash Found 74 Years Later After Disaster Changed Aviation Safety
shortdescription: The wreckage of Pan Am’s Clipper Endeavor, a 1952 plane crash that helped create modern passenger safety briefings, has been discovered underwater off Puerto Rico after 74 years.
author: Rafael O. Medina
seoTitle: Wreckage of Historic Pan Am Plane Crash Found 74 Years Later After Disaster Changed Aviation Safety

content: The wreckage of a Pan American Airways plane that crashed into the Atlantic Ocean in 1952 has been found almost 74 years after the disaster, solving a decades-old aviation mystery and bringing new attention to one of the accidents that helped reshape modern airline safety procedures. The aircraft was called the Pan Am Clipper Endeavour and was located by an exploration team using advanced sonar technology deep underwater off the coast of Puerto Rico.

The discovery was made in tandem with underwater exploration specialists from Deep Sea Vision and the Air/Sea Heritage Foundation. Researchers found the plane's wreckage in the ocean at a depth of about 2,000 feet, including large sections such as the fuselage and tail. The discovery ended years of searching for the aircraft, which had lain hidden beneath the Atlantic since the fatal accident.

The crash of the Pan Am Clipper Endeavour was not just a tragic aviation disaster. It was a turning point in passenger safety. The accident exposed serious deficiencies in emergency preparedness, passenger communication and evacuation procedures at a time when commercial aviation was still developing. The crash taught the aviation industry a lot, including the safety measures that are now standard on every commercial flight, including briefings to passengers on emergency exits, life jackets and evacuation procedures.

Aviation historians and safety experts are intrigued by the find, as it ties a forgotten tragedy from the early days of commercial air travel to procedures that billions of passengers experience daily. Some part of the events surrounding this accident more than seven decades ago influenced what is now a routine safety demonstration before takeoff.

sections.heading: How the 1952 Crash Changed Airline Safety Standards
content: Pan Am Clipper Endeavour disaster The Pan Am Clipper Endeavour disaster occurred on 11 April 1952, when a Douglas DC-4 operating a flight from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to New York crashed. The aircraft had serious mechanical problems, lost engine power shortly after take-off, and the crew had to try an emergency landing in the ocean.

Although the plane was able to make the first water landing, the aftermath was a tragic example of how a survivable crash could turn into a deadly disaster without the proper emergency preparation. All 69 people on board survived the impact at first, according to survivor reports, but many died amid confusion and problems with emergency equipment as the aircraft rapidly sank.

The accident exposed a number of major problems, including the absence of standardised passenger safety demonstrations before flights, a lack of knowledge of emergency evacuation procedures and difficulties with flotation equipment. Most of the passengers were not familiar with the life-saving equipment and did not know how to respond properly during the emergency.

Out of the 69 passengers and crew, only 17 people lived and 52 people died. The tragedy led aviation investigators and regulators to look into how airlines prepare passengers for emergencies, especially those on flights over water.

Aviation authorities began imposing tighter safety requirements in the wake of the crash. It became more and more common for passengers to be given a briefing before take-off and eventually it became mandatory in commercial aviation around the world. The safety culture that created today’s instructions about seat belts, emergency exits, oxygen masks and life vests was born of lessons learned from accidents such as the Clipper Endeavour disaster.

sections.heading: Search Team Solves Decades-Old Aviation Mystery
content: The discovery of the Clipper Endeavour wreckage was the result of years of research, historical investigation and modern underwater technology. Russ Matthews, aviation enthusiast and president of the Air/Sea Heritage Foundation, led the search and began researching the crash site years ago, becoming intrigued by the unsolved mystery of the aircraft’s whereabouts.

Researchers said they narrowed down the aircraft's possible location using historical records, crash reports, ocean mapping data and modern search equipment. The last discovery was made with the help of an autonomous underwater vehicle equipped with a sonar technology that can scan deep areas of the ocean floor.

The team found the aircraft in two main sections on the seabed. Images taken during the exploration revealed identifiable parts of the plane, such as the Pan Am logo, confirming the wreckage was of the Clipper Endeavour. Josh Gates, the explorer who has made his name in underwater and historical finds, also helped in the search. The upcoming episode of the television series Expedition Unknown will feature the expedition, documenting the process of finding the aircraft and exploring its historical significance.

It wasn’t just about finding an aircraft for the researchers involved. It was an opportunity to save aviation history and pay tribute to lives lost in one of the events that helped to make air travel safer for the generations to come.

sections.heading: Discovery Brings Closure, and a Reminder of Progress in Aviation Safety
content: Finding the Pan Am Clipper Endeavour has revived interest in the history of commercial aviation and the development of safety standards. But aviation experts say the crash was a tragedy and that lessons learned from such disasters have brought about significant improvements in passenger protection over the decades.

Modern aviation is one of the safest forms of travel, partly because safety regulations have been improved consistently after accidents that exposed flaws in aircraft design, emergency procedures, and passenger communications. The Clipper Endeavour disaster was one of many historic events that helped shape the evolution of today’s aviation safety culture.

The find also has emotional meaning for families tied to those who died in the crash. Indeed, the aircraft went under the sea not long after the accident, and the remains of many victims were never recovered for decades. Finally, the location of the wreck offers a physical link to a tragedy which had been unresolved for generations.

Researchers say the site will be treated more as an underwater memorial than an archaeological find. The wreckage serves as a reminder of the passengers and crew that lost their lives and the significance of the safety improvements that were made following. More than 70 years after the crash, the resting place of the Clipper Endeavour has been discovered. The find closes a chapter in aviation history and illustrates how past tragedies contributed to the safer skies we fly today.
